Poles in the Sultan's Service

Cihangir – Sadyk Pasha and Ludwika Śniadecka

In these lanes lived a Polish novelist who became a pasha; here the first love of the poet Słowacki died, and the Sultan's Polish court painter had his studio.

Theme
Poles in the Sultan's Service
District
Beyoğlu
Period
1861–1876
Visiting
Seen from outside

The story

In 1860s Cihangir, almost as neighbours, lived three characters fit for a novel: a Polish writer with the rank of pasha, the first love of the poet Juliusz Słowacki, and the Sultan's court painter.

Michał Czajkowski, a writer of Cossack novels and veteran of the 1830–31 Uprising, arrived in Istanbul in 1841 as the agent of Prince Adam Jerzy Czartoryski's Hôtel Lambert in Paris. A year later he founded Adampol, today's Polonezköy. To avoid the expulsion Russia demanded, he became an Ottoman subject and a Muslim at the turn of 1849–50, and as Mehmed Sadyk Pasha he commanded the Sultan's Cossack regiment from 1853, with many Polish officers. Ottoman documents show he had a house in Cihangir in the 1860s.

His companion, Ludwika Śniadecka, was the daughter of the Vilnius scholar Jędrzej Śniadecki; the young Słowacki had been in love with her. She died in Cihangir on 22 February 1866 and was buried at Adampol, where her grave remains. Her portrait of 1864, now in the National Museum in Warsaw, was painted by Stanisław Chlebowski – the painter who, some historians say, owed his entry to the Sultan's palace to Sadyk Pasha. Chlebowski had a studio on Sıraselviler until September 1871, then lived and painted in a rented house in nearby Ağa Hamamı Sokağı.

Poles serving the Sultan were not rare. After the Hungarian revolution was crushed in 1849, General Józef Bem (Murad Pasha) and Konstanty Borzęcki (Mustafa Celaleddin Pasha) were among those who took Islam and the Ottoman uniform; Borzęcki wrote a book on the Turks of old and new, published in Istanbul, and was the great-grandfather of the poet Nâzım Hikmet. Czajkowski left for Russia in 1872 and died there in 1886. None of the Cihangir houses has been identified: the pin marks the street, not a building.

How to visit

This is a walk rather than a visit: none of the houses of that time is marked. Walk down Sıraselviler Caddesi from Taksim Square, turn into nearby Ağa Hamamı Sokağı and carry on down through the lanes of Cihangir to the Cihangir Mosque. Its terrace looks over the Bosphorus to the Asian shore; further north, beyond the hills of Beykoz, lies Adampol, where Ludwika was buried. This is a residential area, so please keep your voice down and do not photograph people in windows or doorways.
